articles.title: Irene Montero, dispuesta a que Podemos se una a Frente Amplio con una sola condición: primarias abiertas en las que puedan votar todos
articles.standfirst: Irene Montero anuncia que se presentaría a las primarias para encabezar la candidatura conjunta
articles.summary: Irene Montero anuncia que se presentaría a las primarias para encabezar la candidatura conjunta
articles.body: Podemos está dispuesta a concurrir junto a las formaciones que integran la nueva alianza de Sumar en las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre, pero plantea como condición la celebración de unas primarias abiertas para elegir al cabeza de cartel. La formación morada ha propuesto que el proceso se celebre los días 14 y 15 de octubre, antes de la presentación oficial del nuevo proyecto político. La número dos de Podemos, Irene Montero, ha planteado este lunes la celebración de estas primarias y ha anunciado que participaría en ellas para optar a encabezar la candidatura conjunta. "No hay tiempo que perder y tenemos mucho trabajo que hacer. Y ofrecemos, ofrezco, unas primarias abiertas a que pueda votar todo el mundo los días 14 y 15 de octubre para elegir entre todas esa candidatura de la mayoría social", ha declarado Montero ante los medios. La propuesta se produce en plena negociación sobre la nueva alianza de izquierdas que están construyendo Movimiento Sumar, Izquierda Unida, Más Madrid y los comunes. Estas cuatro formaciones trabajan bajo el nombre de Frente Amplio de cara a las elecciones generales anticipadas y tienen previsto presentar públicamente su proyecto político y a su candidato el próximo 17 de octubre. Podemos todavía no forma parte formalmente de esta alianza, aunque plantea concurrir junto al resto de fuerzas. La celebración de unas primarias abiertas es precisamente una de las condiciones que la formación morada pone sobre la mesa para incorporarse al proyecto conjunto. El calendario propuesto por Podemos situaría las primarias apenas dos días antes de la presentación prevista por el Frente Amplio. Irene Montero se presentaría a ese proceso para optar a encabezar la candidatura, aunque todavía no está cerrado cómo se resolverá la negociación entre las distintas formaciones. Mientras Podemos plantea sus primarias, las cuatro formaciones que ya integran el Frente Amplio siguen sin haber anunciado quién encabezará su candidatura. Movimiento Sumar, IU, Más Madrid y los comunes tienen previsto presentar el próximo 17 de octubre tanto al cabeza de lista como las líneas principales de su nuevo proyecto político. La incorporación de Podemos es uno de los asuntos pendientes en la configuración de esta candidatura conjunta. La formación morada defiende que la elección del candidato se realice mediante unas primarias abiertas en las que pueda participar la ciudadanía.

articles.title: Inside the Democratic effort to fight any Trump disruption of midterms
articles.summary: House Democrats are preparing legal strategies to challenge any efforts by the Trump administration to disrupt midterm voting or otherwise corrupt the election results. Heading into November, President Trump has sought a greater federal role — and new federal limits — over the election process, which is typically controlled by states, raising concerns in the…
articles.body:
House Democrats are preparing legal strategies to challenge any efforts by the Trump administration to disrupt midterm voting or otherwise corrupt the election results.

Heading into November, President Trump has sought a greater federal role — and new federal limits — over the election process, which is typically controlled by states, raising concerns in the party that he will try to use his powers to tip the scales in favor of Republicans.

Working behind the scenes, teams of Democrats have gamed out a massive list of potential threats to a fair election, identifying roughly 150 different scenarios of potential interference they’re hoping to prevent.

On one front, the lawmakers are coordinating with a host of outside watchdog groups to offer legal resources to local election officials.

On another, some of those lawmakers are barnstorming the country to brief voters and election workers about their rights at the polls.

“We both have our own lawyers, and there are also lots of lawyers throughout civil society who are prepared as much as possible for every eventuality,” said Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), a former constitutional law professor who’s helping with the effort. “We don’t discount or undermine what Donald Trump is capable of. We saw in 2020 a dozen different plans they had to try to thwart democratic sovereignty [over] the election.”

While Democrats are largely focused on winning races in a midterm year when they’re increasingly bullish they can capture both the House and Senate majorities, the under-the-radar efforts underscore deep fears within the party that the Trump administration will seek to subvert the election results if Democrats prevail.

Driving those fears are Trump’s actions after the 2020 presidential election, when he rejected his defeat and inspired a mob of supporters to attack the U.S. Capitol in a failed effort to overturn the results.

“I take seriously that Trump will reject the results if it’s not [in his favor],” said Rep. Bennie Thompson (Miss.), the senior Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee.

Leading one part of the effort is Rep. Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the House Administration Committee, who is taking the reins of the coordination and education efforts, which have already featured more than 15 “shadow hearings” in House districts around the country. A prominent example: If the administration attempts to seize ballots in a contested district “we would have already educated to make sure local officials know the law,” said a source familiar with the effort.

Leading another group is Rep. Joe Neguse (D-Colo.), who heads the Democrats’ litigation task force focused on the party’s legal response to potential threats.

“We’ve got everything ready to be filed. We’ve got documents. We know the arguments. We’ve got the briefs already written,” said Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.). “So we’ve taken all the precautions we can.”

Another scenario relates to the suggestion by top administration officials that they might send federal law enforcers — including FBI and U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents — to polling precincts. Democrats are quick to point out that federal law bars anyone from carrying firearms at polling sites — and they’re racing to ensure that election officials know it, too.

“These are just the standard rules that apply to any election, not just the midterm election. So we’re just trying to assure people that there’s nothing out here going on that you should be concerned about,” Thompson said. “And to be honest with you, the plus side to the concern is that some people are saying, ‘I want to vote early, because I don’t want to deal with the mess.’”

Trump and other top Republican leaders have rejected any accusation that they’re seeking an unfair, or illegal, advantage at the polls. They say they’re simply fighting to eliminate election fraud, which Trump has long claimed is rampant, including their effort to adopt new photo ID requirements for voting.

In a primetime speech from the White House in July, Trump warned of “shocking vulnerabilities in our election infrastructure” that had allowed China to interfere in past elections and threaten to empower noncitizens to impact the midterms.

“Every American deserves to know that when they cast their vote, that vote will be counted accurately in a system, and that is to make that system secure — one where cheating and interference are not just difficult, but virtually impossible,” he said. “Unfortunately, the system we have today falls catastrophically short of that standard.”

The president has not provided any evidence behind his fraud claims, however, and numerous studies across multiple election cycles have revealed that the problem is exceedingly rare.

With that in mind, Democrats say Trump is invoking fraud merely as a pretense to adopt tougher rules that will discourage voter participation for the benefit of Republican candidates.

“We are very well aware that all they have is a bag of dirty tricks at this point,” Raskin said.

Democrats have already won several victories in the courts, which have repeatedly blocked the administration’s efforts to force state officials to turn over their voter rolls. More recently, the Supreme Court halted Trump’s effort to install tough new restrictions on mail-in ballots, which were used by roughly a third of all voters in 2024.

Democrats have been encouraged by those rulings, predicting the courts will also side against Trump if he tries to interfere again.

“The efforts have been transparent, by the White House, trying to interfere,” Lynch said. “So I feel like there’s a solid legal argument against all of that.”

Still, Democrats are also taking nothing for granted. And their preparations heading into November are being done under the assumption that Trump will not deny the results if Democrats win but might also try to overturn them.

“There’s no constitutional mechanism by which he could do it, but there are certainly mechanisms in life that someone like President Trump would try, as we saw on Jan. 6, 2021,” Raskin said. “So we are preparing, not just for the things he might try within our constitutional system — which we feel very confident we would be able to win on — but also things he would try outside of it.”

articles.title: GOP senators, blindsided by Hegseth, demand notice, transparency
articles.summary: Key Republican senators say they were blindsided by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announced 20 percent reduction of the U.S. military’s general and admirals, and they’re voicing concerns about the lack of consultation with Congress and the possibility that qualified senior officers were sacked for political or ideological reasons. Senior Republicans on Capitol Hill are questioning…
articles.body:
Key Republican senators say they were blindsided by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announced 20 percent reduction of the U.S. military’s general and admirals, and they’re voicing concerns about the lack of consultation with Congress and the possibility that qualified senior officers were sacked for political or ideological reasons.

Senior Republicans on Capitol Hill are questioning whether too many experienced and highly qualified generals and admirals are being pushed out because of politics and what impact it might have on military readiness in the future.

“I wouldn’t have made that a priority if I had been asked,” said Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), who said he was only informed of the 20 percent reduction shortly before it was announced.

“I didn’t get a long lead,” he said when asked if he got a heads up before Hegseth’s announcement Wednesday.

Wicker didn’t have many details about the significant reduction in senior ranks. “I think he’s probably interested in cutting out bureaucracy at the top level,” he speculated.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is handling the Pentagon’s request for an emergency supplemental spending package as well as the annual defense spending bill, said the sudden and large reduction of generals and admirals raises questions and concerns.

Collins said she didn’t get advanced notice of the steep reduction in military leadership ranks.

She noted she told Hegseth at a hearing earlier this year that his ouster of senior military officials was “deeply troubling” and risked “depriving us” of the “talent, dedication and patriotism” of women and people of color who were disproportionately pushed out.

On Wednesday, Collins reiterated her argument that “our system for promoting officers has always been an example of one of the greatest meritocracies that we have.”

“I think that we should adhere to a system that has served us well,” she said. “There may be a need to reduce the overall number of flag officers at the Pentagon, but this approach seems to be targeted on ideology.”

“It also disturbs me that there’s a disproportionate number of Blacks and females who are not being promoted,” she added.

GOP senators say Hegseth’s failure to consult with them is part a broader, troubling trend of making big decisions with little or no input from key members of Congress — or even without giving lawmakers sufficient advanced notice.

“Too much time has passed, and he’s failed to respect Congress. He’s never really given us fulsome briefings,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who served eight years on the Senate Armed Services Committee.

“When you’re the head of the Department of Defense or any agency, you at least engage your committees,” he said. “When you hear Sen. Wicker and other people express frustration — we’re his stakeholders. We control his purse strings, and he’s almost treating us like we’re some line workers down in the manufacturing facility that he doesn’t want to spend time with.”

“It’s a huge problem, and I think he’s the face of the problem,” he said.

A Pentagon official dismissed claims that promotions and forced retirements were based on identity politics.

“It is untrue that Secretary Hegseth is basing promotion decisions on race and sex, and we have said so repeatedly,” the official told The Hill.

Hegseth last week defended the reduction in senior officers’ ranks as promoting “accountability” and “long overdue.”

“You can’t change a culture with the same people who enabled it. Personnel is policy at every single level,” he declared at the State of the Force address at the Marine Corps Base in Quantico, Va., and confirmed a 20 percent reduction in generals and admirals “across the board.”

Hegseth also reported that recruiting and retention rates are setting records.

“Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, Space Force, National Guard, reserves, pilots, Special Forces, all setting decades-long recruiting records,” he said.

But the ouster of many experienced and highly qualified officers with little input from Congress has alarmed GOP lawmakers on key committees.

Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), a senior member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hegseth did not consult with Republican or Democratic senators on the key oversight and appropriations committees before moving forward with his plan to slash U.S. military leadership roles.

She confirmed that GOP senators were surprised by the move.

“What I want to see is a plan. I’m not going to say a 20 percent reduction is not warranted. The problem is that the secretary did not come and explain this to us before acting on it, much like a lot of the firings that we’ve seen with military personnel,” she said.

“Are these positions that need to be modernized or collapsed? I want to know that, what’s the reason is behind it?” she said.

Ernst said Hegseth also needs to look at the “civilian population at the Department of Defense” if the goal of pushing out generals and admirals is to reduce bureaucracy.

“We should look at both military and nonmilitary people, but I do have concerns,” she said.

Ernst said reductions in senior military positions need to be justified by evolving military needs and readiness requirements.

She said the departures of high-profile Black and female leaders have created an appearance that they may have been “targeted” for political reasons, namely Hegseth’s high-profile effort to root out “woke” policies or efforts to promote diversity, equality and inclusion.

Hegseth assured the audience during his address at Quantico that the Pentagon remains “colorblind, gender-neutral and merit-based,” but parts of his speech only further raised concerns among GOP lawmakers.

“We are no longer the woke department of the weak department,” he declared in the address. “Simple translation of that: No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals — just warriors, just tough, ready committed troops.”

Media outlets reported earlier this year that Hegseth intervened to stop the promotion of several Army officers, including two Black men and two female officers who had been on track to become one-star generals.

In June, The New York Times reported that Hegseth blocked the promotion of nine Navy officers who had been selected by a board of senior admirals.

President Trump caused an uproar among Democrats when he fired Gen. Charles Q. Brown Jr. — who was only the second Black general to serve as chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff — in February of last year.

Hegseth defended the decision at the time, calling Brown “not the right man for the moment.”

Hegseth fired Adm. Lisa Franchetti, the first woman to serve as chief of Naval Operations, in February of last year, a move that was criticized by Democratic lawmakers.

He thanked her for her “service and dedication to our country” and praised her career as “distinguished” but made clear that Trump wanted “new leadership that will focus our military on its core mission of deterring, fighting and winning wars.”

The building tension between Hegseth and Republican senators comes as Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is grappling over how to fund the Defense Department before the end of the year in the face of staunch Democratic opposition to the military conflict in Iran.

Senate Republicans also face the challenging task of filling senior vacancies in military leadership created by Hegseth’s ouster of key officials, such as Navy Secretary John Phelan. Hegseth sacked Phelan in April.

GOP sources say that Trump’s nominee to replace Phelan, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, faces a roadblock to confirmation because he needs a special congressional waiver given his recent active service. The waiver needs 60 votes and the support of at least seven Democrats.

Federal law requires a seven-year waiting period before a former military officer can take a top-ranking civilian leadership role at the Pentagon.

articles.title: Ticket prices are making sports fans surly this midterm season
articles.summary: The sports world is getting hit by the affordability crisis, as fans find it increasingly costly to attend games or to even watch them on television. A confluence of factors is pricing many Americans out of the market, economists and sports business experts say. Inflation has made it harder to afford nonessential items and services,…
articles.body:
The sports world is getting hit by the affordability crisis, as fans find it increasingly costly to attend games or to even watch them on television.

A confluence of factors is pricing many Americans out of the market, economists and sports business experts say.

Inflation has made it harder to afford nonessential items and services, even as ticket prices across the sports landscape have risen. That’s to say nothing of the costs for concessions or getting to a game.

The at-home sports viewing experience is becoming more expensive, too, with subscriptions to paywalled streaming services increasingly becoming the only way to see every game a favorite team plays.

And none of this has stopped billionaire sports ownership groups from asking the public at large to foot the bill for their stadiums with the threat of leaving town.

The trend line threatens to erode sports fandom’s place in American culture, a growing number of observers say. It’s also another reason why voters in general are in a surly mood this midterm season.

“There were already tensions around big time sports and affordability before we got to this point in the country, but now everything that’s going on with Congress and geopolitical tensions just sort of amplifies it,” said Loretta Lepore, a Republican communications strategist. “And lawmakers in both parties see this. There’s a recognition that we have a growing disparity of wealth in our nation, and it’s creeping into every segment of our society, including sports.”

Affordability for fans was a point of contention when lawmakers in the Senate last week debated the Protect College Sports Act, a controversial proposal seeking to regulate the billion-dollar industry of intercollegiate athletics.

An amendment to the bill, introduced by Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), aimed to cap the amount NCAA member schools can raise ticket prices on a yearly basis at 4 percent.

Kennedy’s amendment was narrowly defeated while the underlying legislation passed.

Leaders at top colleges and executives at pro sports franchises argue higher prices for tickets and amenities are necessary to compete for top on-the-field talent and provide the best possible game-day experience.

“I think when we see a coach making $13 million dollars and you have buyouts … that has to get passed down to somebody in some way,” said Sen. Katie Britt (Ala.), the only Republican who voted in favor of another amendment to cap the salaries of college coaches told The Hill.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.) earlier this year introduced the For the Fans Act, a bill that would regulate the way the NFL, the country’s most popular sports league, negotiates its media deals with streaming services in mind.

Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) told The Hill the Senate Commerce Committee could soon examine price gouging and ticket affordability practices of sports franchises that use public dollars to fund new stadiums and facilities.

“Yes, the cost of being a fan is higher than we’ve ever seen … whether that’s for tickets or food and beverage or merchandise when you’re at the event,” said Brian Berry, executive director of the Ticket Policy Forum.

The growing presence of private equity in major college and pro sports is partly fueling this trend, Berry said, resulting in a new era of sports business where premium seating packages and VIP treatments are being designed to cater to the wealthiest fans, particularly in major markets across the country.

“We’re seeing more and more of these kinds of experientials being offered,” he added. “VIP packages that take you down pregame to the sidelines and that kind of thing. It’s becoming more attractive as an option for these clubs to attract premium customers.”

For fans who opt not to attend games in person, the cost of the at-home viewing experience is also steadily rising.

A study published last month from the economic think tank Groundwork Collaborative found food and beverage items associated with sports viewing cost 10 percent more than they did a year ago — and 13 percent more since President Trump retook office.

Nearly 6 in 10 sports fans said they skipped watching a game on a streaming service because it was too expensive or confusing to locate, the same study found.

“We have built an entertainment economy around sports that really looks like every other business in America. If you’re rich, you’re going to get access to all kinds of experiences regular people just don’t have anymore,” said Alex Jacquez, Groundwork Collaborative’s senior vice president of policy, advocacy and research.

“It’s the same thing with options like Disney World or the movies … all of these things that used to be cornerstones of America’s entertainment, where people could come together and mixed and mingled regardless of class, have just kind of disappeared.”

Despite disagreements on Capitol Hill regarding to what extent the big business of sports should be more regulated, some observers see affordability in sports as low-hanging fruit for lawmakers and a potential area of common ground.

“It seems the political players are looking at this and saying this is a space we can have some bipartisan agreement. It doesn’t matter if you’re a Democrat or a Republican if you want to go watch the Buckeyes or the Yankees or any team it costs the same,” said Nicole Kraft, the director of Ohio State University’s Sports and Society Institute.

“We’re at a place where people feel like sports owe them more than it did before because of how much money they are paying to be there. Those are all pieces that are disrupting sports at the moment, and at this point I’m not sure we have the ability to go back.”

Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) made one of the biggest sports-related gaffes on Capitol Hill in recent memory last week. The Republican lawmaker, as he was questioning former special counsel Jack Smith about what he alleged was his attendance at an Atlanta Hawks game in 2024, apparently confused the NBA team with the Iowa Hawkeyes, who Smith indeed saw play on the same day during the school’s trip to the University of Maryland that year. Text messages from that day, obtained by The Hill , show Smith’s staff didn’t reference any basketball team names as Schmitt had alleged. Republicans have long tried to tie Smith to prosecutors who brought charges against President Trump after he left office in 2020.

The Protect College Sports Act is going to have to wait until after Election Day to get a vote in the House. Republican leadership has repeatedly said there is no chance lawmakers in the lower chamber will return to Washington, D.C., early to consider the bill, which some have suggested cannot pass as it is currently written. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) has floated the idea of the House returning early to work on the legislation before heading back to the trail to “campaign” on the achievement, a move he said would resonate with many “normal people.”

MLB confirmed this week it would not stage a game next season in western Wyoming’s Grand Teton National Park. Commissioner Rob Manfred clarified the league’s position after a Washington Post report suggested MLB had approached the Trump administration about the idea, prompting pushback from environmental groups and other critics. MLB’s future more broadly remains uncertain amid ongoing stalled-out collective bargaining talks between the players’ association and owners, prompting fears of a work stoppage after the conclusion of this month’s postseason.

Jocks on The Hill: Rep. Russell Fry (R-SC)

“University of South Carolina Gamecocks … I have a fantasy team, but I pay attention to college football way more.”

Is there an athlete you admired growing up or even now?

“You know I always appreciated the grittiness of Marcus Lattimore and Connor Shaw, both Gamecocks.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you really like to root against?

“Oh there’s a few of em … nahhh, I think you can guess.”

Sports and politics are full of cliches, what’s one that resonates with you or applies to both?

“Run through the tape and let the coach coach!”

If you’re confused by the scandal in connection with financial crimes by Premier League’s Manchester City, you’re not alone. ESPN has a helpful explainer here laying out what the club was found to have done, what a potential punishment looks like, how the appeals process works and more.

The Athletic published an extensive investigation into the business dealings of Mohamed Coulibaly, an investor at the center of a Ponzi scheme that reportedly duped a number of current and former NFL players out of millions, including former New York Giants linebacker Tae Crowder.

Yahoo Sports’s Dan Wolken has a new column out blasting University of Arkansas men’s basketball coach John Calipari over his recent comments lamenting that many of his players make more than his assistant coaches. Calipari has been one of several college coaches promoting the Protect College Sports Act.

articles.title: Democrat drops 7-figure ad buy in Texas attorney general race
articles.summary: The Democratic candidate for Texas Attorney General launched a seven-figure television ad buy on Monday amid signs of the party’s momentum in the red Lone Star State. Nathan Johnson, a Democratic state senator, argues in the ad that “Texas could use a good lawyer” to replace current Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), the scandal-clad prosecutor…
articles.body:
The Democratic candidate for Texas Attorney General launched a seven-figure television ad buy on Monday amid signs of the party’s momentum in the red Lone Star State.

Nathan Johnson, a Democratic state senator, argues in the ad that “Texas could use a good lawyer” to replace current Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), the scandal-clad prosecutor who’s running in the state’s high-profile Senate race.

The 30-second spot focuses on a May interview with KHOU in which candidate Mayes Middleton, a Republican state senator and oil and gas executive , said he did not think the office had become too political.

“After 12 years of Ken Paxton in office, we need an Attorney General who will put the rule of law over politics and the public good over a personal agenda,” Johnson says in the ad, which is running statewide through Election Day, according to a release from the Democrat’s campaign.

Polling has been sparse in the race, but the latest numbers indicate the race for the typically red seat could be closer than expected.

An August poll from the University of Texas/Texas Politics Project found Middleton up by 5 percentage points, with 40 percent to Johnson’s 35 percent and 21 percent undecided.

A September Texas Southern University poll found Middleton ahead by 5 percentage points, with 47 percent to Johnson’s 42 percent and another 9 percent undecided.

Middleton defeated Rep. Chip Roy (R) in a contentious runoff as he touted his alignment with President Trump. Johnson also won a runoff as he promised to reform the office.

They’re jostling to replace Paxton, whom Democrats have long accused of politicizing the office as he moved aggressively to challenge the Biden administration and support Trump into his second term. Paxton’s tenure as the state’s top law enforcement official has also been plagued by controversy, including an unsuccessful 2023 impeachment on corruption charges.

Johnson contended in a release from his campaign that Paxton turned the office into “a private law firm for the far right.”

Middleton, however, has previously said “the most important thing in the attorney general’s role is defeating the left.”

The Texas attorney general’s office has played a key role in shaping conservative politics — and it’s also served as a political springboard for higher office, with an alumni list that includes Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Gov. Greg Abbott (R).

Though Middleton maintains the polling lead, the race comes against the backdrop of a promising political environment for Texas Democrats, who have struggled for decades to pull off a statewide win.

The Texas Senate race is now a toss-up, according to Decision Desk HQ, with Paxton trailing state Rep. James Talarico (D) in the latest polling averages.

articles.title: Congressional acuity test? Some lawmakers want to talk about age, absences
articles.summary: Calls for congressional reform have bubbled up on both sides of the aisle after two lawmakers’ months-long absences fueled debate over what to do when lawmakers go missing. With regular reminders that this is one of the oldest Congresses in U.S. history — Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley (Iowa), 93, contended with his own…
articles.body:
Calls for congressional reform have bubbled up on both sides of the aisle after two lawmakers’ months-long absences fueled debate over what to do when lawmakers go missing.

With regular reminders that this is one of the oldest Congresses in U.S. history — Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley (Iowa), 93, contended with his own death in discussing his state’s gubernatorial race over the weekend — some lawmakers in both parties are calling for action.

“America is tired of seeing these guys and gals up here that don’t show up and are gone mentally and physically,” Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) said, calling for changes to Congress’s rules on absences and incapacitation.

Still, just one bill has been introduced this year seeking to address absences. The legislation, introduced by Democratic Reps. Seth Moulton (Mass.) and Ritchie Torres (N.Y.) would mandate disclosures of absences longer than 21 days. It has picked up little steam despite uproar over Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) and Rep. Tom Kean Jr.’s (R-N.J.) long absences from Washington due to health issues this summer .

“This institution needs reform. Everyone in America knows that,” Moulton told The Hill.

Lack of reform ‘antithetical to our democracy’

Extended absence from the Capitol is not new, nor is it limited to one party. Although the number of missed votes among legislators has not dramatically jumped in recent years, a number of high-profile, long-term absences and concerns over older elected officials’ ability to serve have sparked scrutiny and calls for change in recent years.

In 2023, former Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) missed 91 votes , and her deteriorating condition garnered calls for her resignation. Former Rep. Kay Granger (R-Texas) missed more than 76 percent of votes in her last months in office before her office confirmed she had been living in an assisted living facility . And in 2024, concerns over former President Biden’s age and health effectively torpedoed his reelection bid.

This year, Kean’s more than 116-day absence from Washington, due to a hospitalization for depression, and McConnell’s months away from Capitol Hill after a fall raised questions about their capacity to serve.

Most Americans believe reform in Congress is needed, with a Marist poll in May showing 8 in 10 Americans favor an age cap and term limits for members of Congress. American approval of Congress also remains poor, with only 16 percent of Americans approving of the way Congress is handling its job.

Any major changes to Congress and its elections would require a constitutional amendment, a notoriously herculean effort that has only succeeded 27 times in U.S. history.

Burchett previously called for a constitutional amendment addressing incapacitation on Capitol Hill, but Moulton and Torres’s bill marks the most recent effort to address the issue within the halls of Congress.

John Martin, a professor of law at Quinnipiac University, has proposed amending the Constitution with a mechanism to replace a member if they are unable to discharge the duties of their office.

“There presently exist no practical means of ensuring that representation continues undisrupted for affected constituents. This is antithetical to our democracy. And with Congress’s average age on the rise, the problem may only get worse,” Martin wrote.

Using the 25th Amendment — which offers a framework to address an incapacitated president — as a blueprint, Martin proposes allowing lawmakers to relinquish their duties to a temporary appointee of the same political party until they are able to return. The proposal would also allow state legislatures to remove an incapacitated member and establish a Congressional Medical Oversight Board to make final decisions on a legislator’s return to office.

“Why don’t we just have something similar for Congress as we already do for the president?” Martin said.

Some political figures have taken this call a step further, arguing for term limits across the executive, legislative and judicial branches.

“We all deserve senators that can actually do their job,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), a leading critic of McConnell’s absence, told ABC’s “The View” earlier this month. “And I think it’s fair to say we can now all agree it’s time for term limits for Congress, and I’ll throw it out, for the Supreme Court too.”

Proposals that don’t involve amending the Constitution may be more feasible, but they still have not garnered much support among lawmakers.

The Duty of Transparency Act, introduced by Moulton and Torres in July, aims to increase transparency by requiring disclosure of the reason for and expected length of absences, as well as updates to those disclosures every 30 days while not participating in congressional proceedings.

There are models for reform in similar legislative branches elsewhere in the world.

In the Australian Parliament, a seat can be vacated after two consecutive absent months, while the Canadian Parliament can reduce members’ salaries if they are gone for more than 21 days. In Mexico, all legislators are elected alongside an alternate who stands by to take over in the event of an unexcused absence longer than 10 days.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), who had a stroke while in office in 2022, told The Hill that a congressional rule change focused on transparency should be “embraced.”

“It’s important to share with your colleagues what happened; it’s most essential and critical to share with your constituents,” Luján said. “The people entrusted you to be here, whether they voted for you or not, you have an obligation to the people back home.”

Luján said while he isn’t familiar with the Moulton-Torres legislation, he would support a change, particularly one that extended to all three branches of government.

“If there’s a change of rules, a change of ethics, not just in the legislative branch but in the White House and in the Supreme Court — that is something that everyone should embrace,” the New Mexico Democrat said. “We should do it together.”

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) said that although he hasn’t been focused on the issue, he believes dramatic changes in life expectancy have potentially changed some of the calculations America’s Founding Fathers made when shaping the legislative branch. He said Congress has to “think through” the ramifications of those changes.

Some lawmakers, however, expressed opposition to any changes to congressional rules.

“I’m OK with the way things are,” retiring Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) said, noting that there’s “sufficient accountability because of freedom of the press.”

Republican Sen. John Curtis (Utah) pointed out that congressional absences are relatively uncommon, adding that lawmakers’ tenures should be decided by voters.

“I feel like that’s up to the voters,” Curtis said. “I think every member, they’re situations are so unique and different, and they have accountability to their constituents and that’s who should be deciding, not us.”

articles.title: Search suspended for 6 aboard medical flight that went missing near Nantucket: Coast Guard
articles.summary: “Suspending a search is not an easy decision,” Coast Guard Northeast District Commander Matthew Lake said in a statement.
articles.body:
Video above: The U.S. Coast Guard speaks about its efforts to locate the six people aboard the lost plane on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026.

NANTUCKET, Mass. ( WPRI ) — The U.S. Coast Guard announced Sunday night they have suspended their search off the coast of Nantucket for six people who went missing after contact with their plane was lost.

Around 2 a.m. Saturday, the FAA told the Coast Guard that contact had been lost with a Gulfstream G100 aircraft, tail number C-GRJP. The aircraft had six people on board and was flying from Bermuda to Boston. The passengers and crew consisted of four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals.

The aircraft “reportedly declared an emergency prior to the loss of contact,” a spokesperson for the Nantucket Memorial Airport said in a statement obtained by Nexstar’s WPRI. The statement noted that “details regarding the circumstances of the incident remain unconfirmed.”

On Saturday afternoon, they announced that search crews had located debris from the aircraft.

Despite continued search efforts on land and water on Sunday, the Coast Guard elected to call off the search.

“Suspending a search is not an easy decision,” Coast Guard Northeast District Commander Matthew Lake said in a statement. “We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude to our partner agencies who helped support search efforts.”

Over 66 hours of searching, the Coast Guard said it searched roughly 4,445 square miles.

Authorities have not publicly identified those who were aboard the plane.

In a statement posted to social media on Saturday, the Government of Bermuda said it had “been in contact with the families of those on board.”

“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time,” Premier David Burt said in the statement.

articles.title: WATCH: GOP senators skeptical of Bill Gates’ ‘fearmongering’ AI warning as Dems sound alarm
articles.summary: Bill Gates' warning that AI could lead to "a billion deaths" divided senators, with some calling it fear-mongering and others demanding regulation.
articles.body: Senators on Capitol Hill were split on Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates’ warning that artificial intelligence (AI) could lead to "a billion deaths" amid growing controversy over the technology’s direction and rapid growth. Gates is one of several industry giants who have sounded the alarm on AI’s advancements, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. President Donald Trump has pushed back on calls to slow down AI development, arguing a rollback could give an advantage to competitors in the AI race like China. Gates made the claim on NBC’s "Meet the Press" last week when he was asked whether AI could wipe out humanity — as some in the industry have warned is a possibility that could happen within a decade. GOP LAWMAKERS SMELL SOMETHING ELSE BEHIND BIG TECH'S AI DOOMSDAY WARNINGS: 'SOMETHING ELSE GOING ON' "I think that's incredibly irresponsible," Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "That's not as dire as some of the AI officials who have suggested that there was a 10 percent chance of wiping out all of humanity," Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, said. "This is something we have to take very seriously." "What worries me about that prediction is that the Republicans who are in control of the House and the Senate say ‘everybody go home and let AI do whatever they want to do,’" Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said. Cornyn claimed that Gates’ warning risks fueling calls for regulations that could ultimately benefit the biggest players in the AI industry while crowding out smaller competitors. "I mean, he's fearmongering," Cornyn said. "And I worry that it's in pursuit of what's sometimes called regulatory capture, that the government and the public will demand regulation while a handful of prime AI companies are in control and crowd out any competitors." WATCH: AI SAFETY SCARE SPARKS CAP HILL FIGHT OVER GUARDRAILS: 'CHINA'S GOING TO EAT OUR LUNCH' King, however, argued the competition between tech companies gives reason why the government should implement safeguards. "The president seems to think, well, industry will regulate itself. The government shouldn't be involved," King said. "The problem with that is that these companies are engaged in an intense competition." He claimed that companies could then be reluctant to voluntarily slow development or impose their own safeguards if doing so risks allowing competitors to pull ahead in the industry. "They're gonna be forced to make a decision: Should we slow down and put in our own safeguards?" King explained. "But if we do, our competitor across the street won't and [will] get ahead of us, or China will get ahead of us." Republican senators also warned about another concern surrounding the rapid development of AI: Could China pull ahead? BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN "Look, I think we need to use common sense," Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., said. "So we want to develop it. Obviously, we need to stay ahead of adversaries like China, but we need to do it safely. " "I think the administration is generally on the right track in not trying to put a heavy hand on this technology, which is going to be fundamental to our economy and our national security," Cornyn said. The conversations around AI ramped up this month, shortly before both the House and Senate went on recess leading up to the midterm elections. articles.title: Midterm temperature check 30 days out, with DDHQ
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ 30 days away from midterms ▪ Hassett’s hot take on polling ▪ Oil companies v. localities ▪ Moscow ramps up strikes Sunday marked 30 days until Election Day. Democrats are favored to win the House and have a slight edge in the Senate, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ…
articles.body:
Sunday marked 30 days until Election Day. Democrats are favored to win the House and have a slight edge in the Senate, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), which puts the party’s chances at 75 percent in the lower chamber and 54 percent in the upper chamber.

Democrats’ prospects have improved in recent weeks, despite a Senate map heavily stacked against them. A month ago, DDHQ gave the party a 49 percent chance of retaking the Senate and a 67 percent chance of winning back the House.

The generic congressional ballot and President Trump ’s overall approval rating can offer clues about how the parties will fare in the midterms, DDHQ’s chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley told Morning Report. Both indicators have shifted in Democrats’ favor and “haven’t really trended back in any notable way.”

“That’s the big question over the last month here: is if Republicans can do anything to stem the tide of that — bring margins on the generic ballot back a little bit, see Trump’s approval rating increase just a tad,” Skelley said. “Any of that would be, I think, helpful to the GOP.”

When it comes to the Senate, he added, “That’s pretty much a coin flip.”

Across the million simulations in DDHQ’s forecast, Democrats win an average of 51 Senate seats and 234 House seats, representing net gains of four seats in the Senate and 19 seats in the House.

The outcomes in the two chambers are closely linked. A favorable environment for one party can boost its candidates in across the country. DDHQ gives Democrats a 52 percent chance of winning both chambers, while Republicans have a 23 percent chance of holding both. There’s a 1 in 4 chance of split control.

Even with a favorable political environment, Democrats face a steeper climb to a majority in the Senate than in the House.

Democrats need to hold all their current seats and flip another four to win control of the chamber. That means Michigan, where Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed is running to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D), is a must-hold for the party.

El-Sayed has a 71 percent chance of defeating former Rep. Mike Rogers (R), “ but that leaves a very realistic possibility for Mike Rogers to win in the end ,” Skelley said. “So the kind of lead El-Sayed has is far from safe.”

Democrats’ most likely path involves flipping North Carolina — where former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper has an 82 percent chance of winning — and then to win another three of five other highly competitive races.

DDHQ puts Democratic chances of flipping Alaska at 61 percent, Texas at 55 percent, Ohio at 53 percent, Maine at 50 percent and Iowa at 47 percent.

Skelley said Texas is particularly worth watching because Democratic nominee James Talarico is polling better than Beto O’Rourke did at this point in 2018, when Democrats last thought they had a real shot at flipping a Senate seat in the state.

Republicans hold a significant fundraising advantage over Democrats, though, and it remains to be seen how that spending advantage will shape Talarico’s race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton .

Democrats need to net just three seats to reach a 218-seat majority in the House.

Results in certain districts could offer early indicators of the broader electoral outcomes, Skelley said, pointing to Florida as a state that tends to count votes quickly.

He said he will be watching Florida’s 14th and 25th congressional districts, where Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz , respectively, are running for reelection in redrawn districts where majorities voted for Trump in 2024.

If both win reelection, DDHQ puts the probability of Democrats flipping the House at 95 percent. If Republicans win both seats, the GOP’s chances of maintaining control of the lower chamber increase to 67 percent.

In Virginia, a rematch between former Rep. Elaine Luria (D) and incumbent Rep. Jen Kiggans (R) could be a key test of Democratic momentum. If Luria unseats Kiggans, DDHQ gives Democrats an 84 percent chance of flipping the chamber. If Kiggans wins, Republicans have a 61 percent chance of keeping control.

Next door in Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, GOP Rep. Rob Wittman is another incumbent to watch. Skelley noted his district is one of the few that shifted to the left in 2024, when most of the country moved to the right, and that Wittman has a history of outperforming the top of the ticket.

“He ran well ahead of Trump in 2024, but if he is in danger of losing on election night, that’s when you know that the national trends have really trumped that local strength, candidate strength, that he has shown previously,” Skelley said.

Preparing for victory: The Hill’s main man in the House, Mike Lillis, takes a deep dive on how Democrats are preparing to fight Trump if he attempts to use federal powers to interfere with election outcomes.

“I take seriously that Trump will reject the results if it’s not [in his favor],” Rep. Bennie Thompson (Miss.), told Lillis for the story, which is available only to Insiders .

The president is heading to Nebraska to rally for incumbent GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts. The Republican faces a tight race against Dan Osborn, an independent backed by Democrats. Trump’s visit to Grand Island, Neb., on Monday will mark his latest stop in a campaign tour that has hit a surprising number of red states.

All 12 B-1 bombers stationed at the RAF Fairford air base in Gloucestershire, U.K., returned to their home stations Sunday. The Pentagon did not specify the reason behind the decision, but it comes days after an alleged terror threat against the base. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that he believed Iran “played a part” in the foiled attack.

The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded on Monday to three scientists — Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagelfor — for pioneering the field of optogenetics, research into brain circuitry that helped advance treatment of conditions including blindness, depression, addiction and dementia.

An official voting center sign stands outside of a polling location on May 26, 2026, in Dallas. (AP Photo/Gabriela Passos)

LATINO SWING: A new poll shows that Trump’s support among Hispanic voters has plummeted since the 2024 election. The NBC News/Telemundo survey found that 27 percent of respondents approved of the president and 69 percent disapproved.

And nearly 6 in 10 Hispanic voters disapproved of Trump’s handling of border security, while almost 7 in 10 said they disapproved of how he has handled immigration and foreign policy.

“Frankly, it’s the hardest job that I’ve had,” Trump said Wednesday regarding immigration enforcement. “They’ll say you’re too tough or you’re too soft. Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it’s always tough.”

Almost three-fourths of respondents disapproved of how he has handled the economy, and 78 percent said they disapproved of how he has handled the cost of living.

Annual inflation rose from 3 percent in January to 3.4 percent as of last month, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Trump campaigned in 2024 on a platform of affordability and lowering prices, after inflation reached a 40-year high under former President Biden .

Democrats held a 24-point edge over Republicans regarding which party Latino voters want to see control Congress after the midterm elections.

▪ The Hill : Trump’s 2024 support from Hispanic voters dips in new poll

“PARTISAN POLLSTERS:” Kevin Hassett , who heads the National Economic Council, dismissed recent polling showing Americans’ concerns about the economy.

“Ahead of an election cycle, the fact that there’s, you know, possibly partisan pollsters telling us that the people are really, really depressed, it’s a classic Democrat move, and I just don’t buy it,” he told CNN’s Jake Tapper during his “State of the Union” interview Sunday.

An Associated Press/NORC survey found that 73 percent of American adults disapprove of the president’s handling of the economy, and 65 percent directly blame Trump’s policies for higher prices.

A Quinnipiac University poll saw 62 percent of respondents critical of the president’s economy.

Hassett, however, says he doesn’t see the criticisms playing out in the real world.

“Because if it were true, if the polls were any value for thinking about what’s going on with consumers, then we should look at the consumption data and say, ‘Jeez, yeah, that’s right. People aren’t spending.’ But, in fact, the retailers are doing well,” he said.

▪ CNN : Hassett defends Trump economy despite voter concerns on inflation

JUDICIAL BLINDERS: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito said Sunday he avoids giving attention to the president’s praise and likewise ignores Trump’s criticisms toward his peers.

“I put all of that out of my mind. I trust that my colleagues put all of that out of their minds,” he told “Fox News Sunday” host Shannon Bream .

Alito also warned about the “escalation in public rhetoric in general and about the things that people in important positions say about the Supreme Court as a whole and about individual justices,” adding that such commentary can damage Americans’ trust in the country’s highest court.

Alito was also interviewed on CBS over the weekend, as part of a publicity tour for his new book, “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court and Our Country.”

The appearances follow Trump’s recent comments in an interview with Time Magazine and on Truth Social where he expressed regret for his nominations of Justices Amy Coney Barrett , Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh .

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” the president wrote on social media last month, while referring to Alito and Justice Clarence Thomas as “legends.”

The Supreme Court has ruled against Trump’s wishes on a number of issues, including his mail-in voting plan and his executive order ending birthright citizenship .

▪ The Hill : Samuel Alito addresses Trump’s comments about him and fellow Supreme Court justices

INITIAL COUNT: Thomas Giuffra, a lawyer for a former Cornell University student who alleges that she was gang raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024, said he believes there were more than seven men who participated in the alleged assault of his client, referred to as Jane Doe.

“I’m not even sure we have everybody who participated in this assault because my client was blacked out during periods of time, and that’s reported in these statements. We don’t even know the people we have are the people we definitively know,” Giuffra told Tapper during an interview on “State of the Union” Sunday.

“If you ask me, I believe there were more,” he added.

The accused men were all in the fraternity Chi Phi. An alleged screenshot from the night shows a man telling other members that there was “free p—- upstairs.”

The case has also drawn bipartisan support in Congress for stronger protections for sexual violence survivors, The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi reports .

This past week, the Education Department announced it had formally rescinded the Biden-era Title IX interpretation that gave sex-based discrimination protections to students on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.

Critics argue the move weakens protections for sexual assault victims.

The House is holding a pro forma session at 4:30 p.m. EDT.

The Senate is holding a pro forma session at 4:00 p.m. EDT.

Pumpjacks operate in a pasture on Sept. 30, 2024, near Hays, Kan. (AP Photo/Charlie Riedel)

FOSSIL FUEL FURY: The Supreme Court on Monday will hear a case that will determine the future of state and local efforts to recover damages from fossil fuel companies’ role in global warming, The Hill’s Rachel Frazin reports .

The case, Suncor v. Boulder, allowed climate change claims brought by the city and county of Boulder against oil companies to proceed. The justices’ decision could set a precedent to toss other cases around the nation.

Suncor Energy and ExxonMobile asked the Supreme Court to reverse the decision initially made by the Colorado Supreme Court, arguing that federal law preempts state-level cases.

“There is no constitutional bar to states addressing in-state harms caused by out-of-state conduct, be it the negligent design of an automobile or sale of asbestos,” said a brief from the city and county.

“What’s at stake is the future of litigation seeking money damages from fossil fuel companies over climate change, ” said Michael Gerrard , faculty director of Columbia Law School’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law.

If that happens, localities won’t be able to collect funds from climate change contributors and will have to find another way to pay for damages caused by rising sea levels, floods and wildfires.

Gerrard said there are roughly two dozen cases underway.

If these climate lawsuits are successful, it would mean “massive damages that would be very difficult for the companies to pay,” he added.

When the Supreme Court agreed to take up the case this year, justices raised questions about their authority to hear it. If the court rules it can’t, it’s a “punt” and could return at a later date.

Alitorecused himself from the case, as he has financial holdings in other oil companies.

The Trump administration has sided with the oil companies.

COMING ESCALATION: Moscow announced Sunday that it would ramp up strikes against key military facilities across Ukraine, following Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ’s recent threats to target Russian oil refineries.

“Strikes by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation against military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified,” the Russian Defense Ministry wrote on Telegram.

The Telegram statement comes following Zelensky’s interview Saturday with Reuters, where he told the outlet that “with their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war.”

The Russian-Ukraine war, which is well into its fourth year, has taken a toll on the global economy and Trump has blamed Kyiv’s newest strategy targeting refineries for rising diesel prices, which reached record highs last month.

articles.title: On immigration, Democrats should look to the Nordic model
articles.summary: Despite the issue’s enduring salience, few center-left parties have figured out how to defuse it.
articles.body:
As Democrats and other center-left parties struggle to understand why working-class voters have turned against them, they reach readily for economic explanations. Yet most flinch from confronting another potent driver of blue-collar anger — uncontrolled immigration.

Of course, that’s partly an economic issue too. But it also illuminates the deep rift between elite and popular opinion on emotive questions of national sovereignty, cultural identity and democratic agency in deciding who can enter one’s country and become a citizen.

Stopping illegal immigration has been President Trump’s most reliable rallying cry. His call to wall America off from a flood of “criminal aliens” in 2016 helped him forge a strong bond with non-college voters. He went back to the immigration well in his 2024 comeback, when those voters again ranked the issue as a top concern, second only to high living costs .

Hostility to mass migration also is the rocket fuel propelling neo-nationalist populists in Europe. These include the far-right Alternative for Germany party, which recently made startling gains in state elections; France’s National Rally, now leading polls ahead of next year’s presidential election, and the United Kingdom’s fast-rising Reform Party.

Across the West, working-class voters feel betrayed by political elites who lecture them about the aggregate economic benefits of more immigration and belittle their doubts as nativist if not racist. Despite the issue’s enduring salience, few center-left parties have figured out how to defuse it.

Denmark is a conspicuous exception. Since the Social Democrats came to power in 2019, they have slowed the pace of immigration while speeding up deportation of uninvited gate crashers. They have also moved aggressively to integrate migrants into Danish society, passing “parallel society” laws to prevent their concentration in segregated communities.

European progressives have decried the shift as a concession to right-wing xenophobia. But Mette Frederiksen, who won her third term as prime minister last June, maintains that a restrictive migration policy is integral to her party’s historic commitment to social solidarity.

“Being a traditional Social Democratic thinker means you cannot allow everyone who wants to join your society to come,” she told the New York Times . With porous borders, “it’s impossible to have a sustainable society, especially if you are a welfare society, as we are.”

Fredericksen believes admitting fewer migrants and speeding their assimilation into Danish life are key to sustaining public support for the high taxes necessary to support Denmark’s generous welfare state, which corrects for economic inequality. That approach has enabled her party to stem working class defections while marginalizing the hard-right Danish Peoples’ Party.

She also emphasizes a critical point that seems to elude many on the U.S. and European left: The economic and social costs of large-scale immigration — competition for jobs and downward pressure on blue collar wages, gang-related violence, strains on schools, housing, public health and other services — are not distributed evenly. They fall more heavily on wage earners than highly educated and well-heeled Danes.

Center-left governments in other Scandinavian countries are following Denmark’s lead. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store’s “Plan for Norway” includes calls for “clearer and stricter” immigration laws that tighten rules around family unification, speed up deportation of immigrants who don’t qualify for asylum and combat criminal gangs that help people enter the country illegally.

Sweden’s Social Democrats, historically a working-class party, also have executed a U-turn on immigration. “We had one of the most generous asylum systems in Europe, and that was wrong,” admits the party leader Magdalena Andersson , who is working to form a center-left governing coalition.

Democrats, who have long admired the Nordic economic model, should learn from the new Nordic model on immigration. It offers a humane path to curbing illegal migration in contrast to the cruel and violent tactics of Trump and his sadistic henchman Stephen Miller.

The party, however, has yet to reckon with the Biden-Harris administration’s immigration debacle. Biden loosened asylum and parole rules and until 2024 made little effort to secure the border. Migrants saw the green light and surged across it in record numbers .

Voters won’t trust Democrats to enforce immigration laws until they break emphatically with progressive demands for “decriminalization” and open borders. They should recall that Presidents Barack Obama and Bill Clinton kept illegal immigration under control despite taking flak from the left and immigrant rights’ groups for robust deportation programs.

Democrats are keenly attuned to how economic and technological change have undermined working Americans’ prospects for upward mobility. The same forces have sparked the mass migrations of the 21st century — and a furious popular backlash.

To keep faith with their traditional working-class constituents, center-left parties need to show they can control borders, restrict illegal entry and assimilate newcomers in ways consistent with liberal and social democratic principles. The Nordic Model shows that’s not a mission impossible.

Will Marshall is founder and president of Progressive Policy Institute .

articles.title: The oil industry should pay for climate change — and Congress should decide how
articles.summary: For more than 60 years, America’s response to global climate change has been like a hot potato passed from the presidency to Congress and the courts. Now, Congress should end the game once and for all.
articles.body:
For more than 60 years, America’s response to global climate change has been like a hot potato passed from the presidency to Congress and the courts. Now, Congress should end the game once and for all.

The potato tossing began in 1965 when President Lyndon Johnson’s science advisers warned him that fossil-fuel pollution was causing a “vast geophysical experiment” that would alter the Earth’s climate and be “deleterious” to humans. Johnson told Congress, but neither he nor lawmakers acted to control greenhouse gases.

In 1988, one of the government’s principal climate scientists informed Congress that climate change was underway in the United States, caused by human activity and likely to make weather disasters more extreme. Congress responded with several bipartisan climate bills. In 1992, the Senate ratified America’s involvement in the first international climate treaty.

But before long, the fossil energy industry and Republican lawmakers launched a campaign to discredit and deny climate science, causing the issue to become highly partisan. Democratic presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden all attempted to implement climate-action programs, only to have Congress and their Republican successors scuttle them.

Climate change moved into the legal arena in 2004. Eight states and New York City filed the first major lawsuit seeking reductions in carbon dioxide emissions from power plants. The court ruled that only the Environmental Protection Agency could regulate the emissions. So, state, local and tribal governments turned to a different strategy, filing dozens of lawsuits not to limit emissions but to compensate them for climate-related damages .

The lawsuits generally allege that the fossil-energy industry knew for decades that using their products would contribute to climate change, but they concealed the risks and promoted consumption. None of the lawsuits have gone to trial .

Today, the U.S. Supreme Court is hearing one of those cases, Boulder County v. Suncor Energy Inc . The court will not decide whether the county should receive damages; that will be left to later proceedings if the case survives. Instead, the lawsuit tests whether federal law preempts states from climate-damage claims. The court is expected to rule next spring.

Meanwhile, all Americans are paying for climate change with its inflationary effects and its escalating damages. State and local taxpayers pay for the damages, too, along with the legal costs of lawsuits. NOAA reports the U.S. has suffered more than 400 billion-dollar disasters between 1980 and 2024, with total damages reaching nearly $3 trillion .

To add insult to injury, fossil fuel companies received $18.2 billion in implicit subsidies from all levels of government in the U.S. during 2024, plus $1.1 trillion in explicit subsidies — i.e., unpriced social and environmental costs along with foregone revenues. Meanwhile, oil and gas companies continue to rake in record-breaking profits .

This game must stop. Next year, Congress could do the following:

Regulation: Explicitly identify greenhouse gases to be regulated and give EPA unambiguous authority to solve the “major questions” problem.

Liability : Establish when an energy producer can be held liable for climate damages, and how responsibility is apportioned between producers and consumers.

Compensation: Create a federal trust fund for states and localities and require fossil energy companies to pay into it commensurate with their emissions. Precedents include the Hazardous Substance “Superfund,” the Oil Spill Liability Fund and the Black Lung Disability Trust . Assess whether the 1998 tobacco settlement provides a model for states and oil companies.

Future Generations : Define the government’s obligation to future generations and require long-term climate consequences to be incorporated into federal decisions.

Litigation is revealing the problems in federal climate law regarding the damages that fossil fuels impose on the American people. Now, Congress must fix them.

William S. Becker is a former regional director at the U.S. Department of Energy and author of several books on climate change and national disaster policies.

articles.title: Catholic schools, banned rifles and ‘climate lawfare’: Blockbuster fights await Supreme Court
articles.summary: From AR-15 restrictions to Catholic preschool funding, the Supreme Court faces blockbuster cases testing Second Amendment and religious freedom limits.
articles.body: The Supreme Court opens its new term Monday with cases that could reshape religious liberty, gun rights, immigration and the balance between state and federal authority. While the last term was dominated by major cases testing presidential power — including Trump’s authority to restrict birthright citizenship, impose tariffs and fire independent agency officials — many of the court’s marquee cases this term span a wide range of issues, including federalism and individual rights. "There’s a couple of religious freedom cases," Carrie Severino, president of JCN, told Fox News Digital. "We have a couple cases that touch on state and federal preemption, but I’m not sure there’s an easy theme for all of them." The blockbuster case this term is Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, and it centers on whether Colorado officials can use state tort law to seek damages from oil giants Suncor and ExxonMobil for climate-related harms, or whether federal law blocks those claims. SUPREME COURT CLIMATE SHOWDOWN JOLTED BY ALITO'S LAST-MINUTE DECISION "If Colorado actually succeeds on its nuisance claims and others against these companies, the upshot would not just be these companies changing what they do in a way to protect Colorado or remedy Colorado, but rather it would affect their operations far outside of the state," Adam White, senior fellow at American Enterprise Institute, shared during a Federalist Society Panel. "And the question is, can Colorado courts reach outside of their own state and try in effect to regulate?" Suncor and ExxonMobil argue that the Clean Air Act gives the federal government authority over interstate and international emissions, leaving Colorado unable to hold them liable for conduct outside the state. But the state argues that it is seeking damages under state law and that the Clean Air Act preserves states’ authority to enforce their own laws. The Supreme Court will decide whether federal law blocks Boulder’s climate lawsuit and whether the justices can hear the case. Severino said the case is an effort by "climate lawfare activists" to regulate carbon emissions. "If the court is viewing this as an effort to weaponize one jurisdiction's law to really regulate outside its borders, then I think they're going to be not very happy about this claim," Severino said. "If the court really views it as an attempt by Colorado to legislate worldwide actions of these energy companies, then I think they're going to say this is actually something that fits within the federal government's sphere of activity, not a single state." The case marks the first oral arguments heard before the high court. An Arizona election integrity measure is at the center of another Supreme Court case testing the balance of power between states and the federal government over how elections are run. THESE 11 UPCOMING SUPREME COURT DECISIONS COULD MAKE OR BREAK TRUMP'S SECOND TERM AGENDA Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota stems from an Arizona law requiring documentary proof of U.S. citizenship for certain voter registrations. Voters who register without that documentation may qualify as "federal-only" voters, allowing them to vote in federal elections but not state and local races. The law also allows the state to purge noncitizens off voter rolls close to an election. The dispute centers on whether the National Voter Registration Act prevents Arizona from imposing additional requirements on voters. The Supreme Court will also hear major cases involving gun rights and religious liberty and will determine how far states can go in limiting those freedoms. Colorado is up to bat twice before the Supreme Court this term, with St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy testing whether the state can exclude Catholic preschools from its universal preschool program because of religious policies barring same-sex couples and LGBT students from attending the schools, which conflicts with the state’s nondiscrimination requirements. Colorado provides funding to private preschools that participate in the program but requires them to follow state anti-discrimination rules covering sexual orientation and gender identity. The Catholic schools argue those rules clash with their religious beliefs and that they should not have to abandon their policies to receive the same funding available to other private schools. "They don't agree with the state on things like allowing children to use the opposite sex bathroom if they identify with the opposite sex. So this is something the Supreme Court has been very favorable to religious organizations of and for not allowing states to just cut them out of otherwise generally applicable state benefit programs," Severino said. EXCLUSIVE: SUPREME COURT PRAYER GROTTO CASE COULD IMPACT 'EVERY SINGLE ZONING LAW' IN AMERICA, ATTORNEY SAYS But Amanda Shanor, an attorney who helped represent the gay couple who were denied a wedding cake before the Supreme Court, said during a Federalist Society Panel there is concern that the case could chip away at anti-discrimination protections by expanding when businesses and institutions can refuse to serve people based on their identity. "The schools are not saying, like in the earlier cases — like Masterpiece Cake Shop or 303 Creative — that they want to not serve somebody because of the expression that it would express with regard to a particular event, but instead that they don’t want to have the kids or the families because of the status of the kids or the families," Shanor said. "And will that then go spread over into other things, like will the bakery be able to say, ‘I don’t want to serve all X type of people?’" Illinois and Connecticut have cases, with state laws restricting certain semiautomatic firearms facing challenges at the Supreme Court. "This is important because the Supreme Court, for the first time following its landmark Bruen decision, is going to be looking at how states or municipalities can limit particular types of weapons," Severino said. "What the court said it's going to look at is whether these are weapons that are in common use and have lawful purposes, and so this is the court's opportunity to look at things like the popular AR-15 type rifle and decide is this something that qualifies as something that's in common-use and therefore is protected by the Second Amendment." And while presidential power may not be a major theme this term, the Supreme Court will still weigh the limits of the Trump administration’s authority in a case involving its push to deport illegal immigrants to third-world countries they are not from, and that are not listed in their removal orders. The case is not a direct test of presidential power, but instead centers on whether federal immigration law gives the administration the authority to carry out the policy. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) phone number online amid a dispute over permanent daylight saving time, quipping that the president “can go from zero to a‑‑hole in about three seconds.” “Every now and then, there are disputes in Congress that have existential significance for the…
articles.body:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) weighed in Sunday after President Trump posted Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) phone number online amid a dispute over permanent daylight saving time, quipping that the president “can go from zero to a‑‑hole in about three seconds.”

“Every now and then, there are disputes in Congress that have existential significance for the future of Western civilization. Daylight saving time is not one of them,” Kennedy told NBC News’s Kristen Welker Sunday on “Meet the Press.”

“Tom Cotton feels strongly about it. Tom is a rock star senator. If you get between him and what’s best for Arkansas, he’ll devour you like a light snack. President Trump’s also my friend. He feels strongly about it,” he continued. “The president, as we know, can be sometimes — he exists loudly. He can be tempestuous. He can go from zero to a‑‑hole in about three seconds.”

The Louisiana Republican added, “I don’t think he should have given out Tom’s cellphone number. I don’t think that’s going to help convince Tom.”

Trump, who posted the number Saturday on Truth Social, has pressed Cotton to advance legislation to make daylight saving time permanent. The senator, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, has been a vocal opponent of the legislation.

“Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill,” the president wrote. “For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one! It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion.”

“To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself. Call Tom on his cellphone,” he added, before sharing the number. “Let him know.”

Trump has largely blamed Cotton for holding up the Sunshine Protection Act after the bill cleared the House in July via a 308-117 vote.

The Arkansas Republican, in a statement shared on social platform X , said, “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter.”

“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” he concluded.

He has not responded to Trump’s posts sharing his number.
