articles.title: Democrats are poised for a win in the midterms — but can they govern?
articles.summary: If the Democrats win in November, it will be from collecting protest votes, not from offering solutions.
articles.body:
With just under one month until the midterm elections, Democrats hold their largest advantage of the cycle.

Indeed, NBC News’s polling average puts Democrats’ generic ballot lead at 9 points , identical to Nate Silver’s tracker and RealClearPolitics’s aggregate. Gamblers agree: Democrats also show a 62 percent chance of sweeping both chambers on prediction site Kalshi.

Moreover, a New York Times analysis of primaries in Senate battleground states underscores that Democrats are considerably more motivated than Republicans. Compared to 2022, as the article notes, Democrats saw higher turnout in 17 of the 22 states with contested primaries for governor or Senate, whereas Republicans saw lower turnout in two-thirds of such contests.

This happened in red and purple states alike. Nearly 600,000 more Democrats voted than Republicans in Michigan. In Texas, Democrats outvoted Republicans by 150,000 votes, a swing of more than 1 million votes versus 2022.

To be sure, the Democrats’ polling leads come from legitimate concerns voters have with Republicans. Inflation continues eroding Americans’ paychecks — consumer prices rose 3.4 percent year over year for August, outpacing wage gains. The national average for gasoline remains above $4.40 per gallon, more than 30 percent higher than a year ago, and diesel prices — crucial for transportation and farming — are at historic highs , with those costs filtering into food and goods.

Finally, mortgage rates continue to rise , keeping homes unaffordable for millions of Americans.

As a result, Americans feel worse about the economy today than at nearly any point on record. September’s consumer sentiment index from the University of Michigan fell to its second lowest reading since 1952. And President Trump’s approval rating, at 39 percent overall but just 29 percent among independents, is historically low , per Emerson polling.

Democrats are right to run on these issues, and their lead is earned. The grievances behind it are real and widespread, and the party has correctly diagnosed Republicans’ vulnerabilities.

That said, the question remains: If the Democrats win, what will they do to best position themselves for 2028? Because if the Democrats do win, it will be from collecting protest votes, not from offering solutions.

The data bears this out. According to NBC , a plurality (46 percent) of independents said their midterm vote will be “a signal of opposition to the president.”

That same survey also found that the Democratic Party’s favorability (net negative 21 points) is noticeably worse than Republicans’ net negative 13 points, leading the pollster to concede that Democrats “remain in a terrible position as a brand nationally.”

Consider how unusual that is. Democrats are on the verge of winning one or both chambers, yet voters like Republicans more.

There are emerging signs that Democrats, aware of their branding struggles, are concerned.

Adam Hamilton, Democrats’ Senate nominee in Kansas, recently said he does not want former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigning with him , because she “is not somebody who would win votes here.” Hamilton’s calculation is understandable: He needs crossover votes in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in more than 90 years.

Other Democrats in red and purple states have echoed those concerns, making for an awkward dynamic highlighting challenges in areas Democrats need to win the presidency.

To that end, Democrats’ advantage partly rests on factors outside their control — Trump, inflation, affordability — yet they have not coherently put forward an agenda addressing these issues, like the Republicans’ 1994 “ Contract with America ” or Democrats’ “ Six for ’06 ” plan did.

Midterms do not often demand a proactive agenda: Democrats gained 41 House seats in 2018 largely on protecting the Affordable Care Act, and Republicans gained 63 in 2010 due to anger toward then-President Barack Obama.

That said, the ground is different for Democrats in 2026.

There is no true standard bearer or clear direction amid the party’s ideological split, and even winning both chambers won’t allow Democrats to do many of the things they’re campaigning on.

Yes, they will be able to subpoena and stall Trump’s legislative priorities, but he has shown a willingness to go around Congress, and Democrats will be the ones held accountable for a dysfunctional legislature. Voters, having cast ballots over costs and inflation, will judge the new majority against those issues, which Democrats will largely be powerless to address.

If all Democrats have to show for their majority are impeachment hearings by mid-2027, any momentum or “goodwill” will exhaust itself before the 2028 cycle begins. This will be especially true as Trump sinks into lame-duck status and can no longer be either party’s sole unifying force. A majority assembled on someone else’s unpopularity produces no mandate for Democrats.

In that same vein, a victory in November would merely postpone the ideological battle between progressives and moderates, not resolve it.

Ultimately, Democrats are likely to win in November. Frustration with the president should be enough to hand Democrats the Speakers’ gavel, but it won’t hand them the White House in 2028 unless they can tell voters why they’re the right party to lead — not only that the other party can’t be trusted.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die. ”

articles.title: Bolsonaro favourite to win: What Brazil’s first round of elections tells us
articles.summary: Analysts say Flavio Bolsonaro is projected to win the run-off vote on October 25 and become Brazil’s next president.
articles.body:
Right-wing Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has exceeded expectations in the first-round vote with a slight lead over the incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio ‌Lula da Silva, triggering a run-off later this month.

“Brazil wants change, and I am very happy with the results,” Bolsonaro told reporters in Brasilia on Sunday as he saluted “the end of the era of [Lula’s] Workers’ Party”.

The 45-year-old ⁠son of right-wing former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year jail sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, now faces an October 25 showdown with the 80-year-old Lula, who is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term.

‌In the run-up to Sunday’s first-round vote, a series of polls showed a close race between Lula and Bolsonaro, with the incumbent president poised to win by about 3 percentage points against his right-wing challenger.

In a surprise result that defied opinion poll projections, Bolsonaro beat Lula with 47 percent of the vote, while Lula got 45.1 percent.

Neither reached the 50 percent threshold needed to win in the first round. That sets up another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown, four years after Lula narrowly defeated Jair Bolsonaro.

Why is Bolsonaro favoured to win Brazil’s election?

Bolsonaro’s stronger-than-expected performance is likely to buoy his campaign and may bolster Brazil’s currency and stock market, which have risen on the prospects of the business-friendly challenger.

Oliver Stuenkel, professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) in San Paulo, Brazil, said Lula was in a difficult position as he could not count on voters who backed one of the other 10 candidates to vote for him in the second round.

“Not only is he behind now after this first round, but the other candidates who received a total of nearly 8 percent are largely centre-right, which means that the people who voted for these other candidates are very unlikely to shift for Lula,” Stuenkel told Al Jazeera.

“So he must change his campaign tactics and above all mobilise a significant part of people who stayed at home,” he added. About 30 million Brazilians – 21 percent of the electorate – did not vote in the first round.

Al Jazeera’s Monica Yanakiew, reporting from Rio de Janeiro, said Lula supporters felt their candidate had not used social media as effectively as the right-wing camp. “This is something they have to work on in the second round,” Yanakiew said.

From a historical perspective, however, such efforts are unlikely to change the outcome. “Unless something very unusual happens in the next three weeks, Flavio Bolsonaro is set to win,” Stuenkel said. “In Brazilian presidential politics, no candidate who came second in the first round ended up winning the presidency since 1989.”

Has the Bolsonaro family taken hold of Brazil?

Several politicians from the Bolsonaro family have won congressional races taking place as part of the broader nationwide general elections.

Michelle Bolsonaro, wife of former President Jair Bolsonaro and stepmother of Flavio, won a Senate seat in the Federal District, home to the capital, Brasilia.

In June, the 44-year-old, who has never held government office, had a public falling out with her stepson, whom she accused of disrespecting her in lengthy videos posted on her social media. The pair later made up.

Ex-leader Bolsonaro’s second son Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, was the second most-voted senatorial candidate in the southern Santa Catarina state and won a seat in the Senate.

The fourth and younger son, Jair Renan Bolsonaro, was elected to the lower house of Congress.

Some experts credit “antipetismo” — a trend of hostility against Lula’s PT movement — with fuelling the Bolsonaro family’s rise to political power.

Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) won 121 of the 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies while Lula’s PT got 70.

What are the implications of a Bolsonaro win?

Brazil’s presidential election carries significant regional and geopolitical implications.

Reporting from Sao Paulo, Al Jazeera’s Lucia Newman said Lula has been “on a collision course” with United States President Donald Trump, who is a vocal and ardent supporter of the Bolsonaro camp.

“That puts Brazil in the middle of a fierce competition between Washington and China for political, diplomatic and economic dominance, especially since Brazil is a powerhouse on all these fronts,” Newman said.

While Bolsonarism is strongly aligned with the US and Israel, Brazil also has a tight economic relationship with China, its largest trade partner. Bolsonaro has portrayed Trump as an ally and is expected to strengthen ties with Washington if elected.

In case of a win, the younger Bolsonaro has pledged to seek a congressional amnesty for his father, who is in prison over his role in a coup plot following his election loss to Lula by 1.8 percentage points in 2022. That would need approval from both houses of Congress, which are currently dominated by conservatives.

Similar to Trump, the Bolsonaros have made rigged election claims. The insurrection that shook Brasilia in January 2023 shared similarities with the storming of the US Capitol two years prior. Like Trump, Bolsonaro has also pledged to release his father’s supporters responsible for the coup.

Concerns about US intervention in Brazil’s domestic affairs have also loomed over the campaign. Lula has accused the Trump administration of using tariffs and other means to interfere with Brazilian affairs.

Vinicius de Carvalho, a lecturer in Brazilian studies at King’s College London, UK, stressed that Latin America has been experiencing a right-wing wave, with the election of US-aligned governments. This includes Ecuador, El Salvador, Panama and Paraguay.

By contrast, Lula was part of the so-called “pink tide” in Latin America, a wave of left-leaning governments that came to power in the late 1990s and early 2000s. With Congress stacked against him, if Lula is re-elected, he will still need to “respond to some demands of the right”, de Carvalho said.

articles.title: Karoline Leavitt’s next career move revealed after exit as Trump’s press secretary
articles.summary: Leavitt left her post as Trump’s press secretary at the end of August
articles.body:
Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt has landed her next job after leaving the Trump administration.

Leavitt, who stepped down from her post at the end of August , had remained tight-lipped about her plans for what came next.

But now, Fox News has announced that the 29-year-old will be joining the network as an on-air contributor from November 1. She is expected to appear on multiple shows on the network, providing commentary across opinion and news programs.

Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott said in a statement: "Karoline's firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today's political landscape. We look forward to her providing our audience with authentic and sharp insight across all Fox News Media platforms."

Leavitt added in a statement of her own: "I am grateful for the opportunity to continue appearing on Fox News Channel as an official member of the extraordinary team at Fox News Media. I look forward to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House Press Secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defied my tenure, to Fox's millions of viewers across their many platforms."

Leavitt announced her departure from the White House just weeks after returning from maternity leave following the birth of her second child. She shares her two children, a son and a daughter, with her husband, Nicholas Riccio , 60.

A replacement for Leavitt has yet to be announced.

In announcing her departure from his administration, Trump wrote in an August post on Truth Social that Leavitt was leaving in order to "spend more time with her beautiful young children and family , a decision I totally understand and respect."

Leavitt called the role the "honor and adventure of a lifetime."

In a lengthy statement on X, Leavitt claimed the U.S. is facing an "existential threat from an increasingly extremist Democrat Party that seeks to destroy everything great about America" as she embraced her upcoming role as a "top advisor" to the president "on the outside" as well as a "vocal advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party."

She continued: "The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary — and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life."

Before her time at the White House ended, Leavitt announced that she would return to work for MAGA Inc . She served as a spokesperson for the pro-Trump super PAC before joining Trump's 2024 presidential campaign and later the White House press team.

News of Leavitt's Fox gig comes just days after a report indicated that the former press secretary is shopping a book about her tenure to publishers.

articles.title: Disgraced former House Speaker Dennis Hastert dies at 84
articles.summary: Former Rep. Dennis Hastert, who spent eight years as House speaker and later served prison time for scheming to cover up sexual abuse allegations, is dead.
articles.body: Former Rep. Dennis Hastert, who served eight years as speaker of the House — longer than any Republican in U.S. history — and then spent more than a year in prison after he left Congress for scheming to cover up sexual abuse allegations, died over the weekend, according to the Kendall County Coroner’s Office in Illinois. He was 84. “Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell confirmed that over the weekend, former US House Speaker John Dennis Hastert passed away at his home due to natural causes,” the coroner’s office said in a Monday statement. “No further information is available for release.” Hastert, of Illinois, served in the House from 1987 to 2007 and became speaker in 1999. He relinquished the speaker's gavel in 2007 after Democrats took control of the chamber, then announced his resignation from Congress before the end of his 11th term. Nearly a decade later, Hastert faced allegations that he molested four teenagers, ages 14 to 17, in the 1970s, when he was a wrestling coach at Yorkville High School in Illinois. Hastert never faced sexual abuse charges because the statute of limitations had expired. But in 2015, he pleaded guilty to structuring cash withdrawals to hide hush money payments to one of his sexual abuse accusers. The following year, he was sentenced to 15 months in prison. He was released from a prison hospital in 2017, several weeks ahead of schedule. At his sentencing hearing in 2016, Hastert said he was “deeply ashamed” of his actions, adding, “I’m the only one responsible,” NBC Chicago reported. “I know I am here because I mistreated some of the athletes I coached,” he said. “The thing I want to do is say I’m sorry.” U.S. District Judge Thomas Durkin called Hastert a “serial child molester.” One of the accusers, Scott Cross, said in court that Hastert sexually abused him during his senior year in high school. “I’ve always felt that what Coach Hastert had done to me was my darkest secret,” Cross said. When he was released from prison, he was banned from being alone with children or having pornography. His sentence also included two years of supervised release and a $250,000 fine. It was a stunning fall for a veteran politician who was once one of the most powerful people in Washington. During his political career, Hastert had talked up his time as a coach, saying it meshed with politics. “Throughout his legislative career, Speaker Hastert has drawn from his experience as a former wrestling coach by emphasizing teambuilding and setting clear-cut, achievable goals,” said a 2004 web archive of Hastert’s biographical webpage. During Hastert’s time in Congress, he strongly supported the Iraq War and was a champion of then-President George W. Bush’s tax cuts and a Medicare prescription drug bill. The measure, passed in 2003, was sponsored by Hastert. It established an optional prescription drug benefit program that took effect in 2006. Hastert also became the namesake of the unofficial "Hastert Rule," which says the speaker should bring legislation to the floor only if it is supported by “the majority of the majority.” That is, a speaker should call a bill up for a vote only if most of their caucus is in favor of passing it. Hastert was preceded as House speaker by Rep. Newt Gingrich, R-Ga., and succeeded by Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif. Born in Aurora, Illinois, in 1942, Hastert attended Wheaton College, where he earned a B.A. in economics, and then Northern Illinois University for a master’s degree in education. Before being elected to Congress in 1986, he was a member of the Illinois state House of Representatives. He was also a teacher, coach and business owner. Hastert was named Coach of the Year in 1976 by the Illinois Wrestling Coaches and Officials Association. The same year, he served as president of the National Wrestling Conference, according to the IWCOA website. In 2016, the National Wrestling Hall of Fame revoked honors it had given to Hastert, who had been inducted to the hall of fame in 2003. In 2015, then-House Speaker Paul Ryan, R-Wis., had Hastert's portrait removed from a hallway in the Capitol. The removal of the portrait — one of Ryan's first acts as speaker — came shortly after Hastert pleaded guilty.

articles.title: Highest-ranking US official to ever serve jail time, former House Speaker Dennis Hastert dead at 84
articles.summary: Former House Speaker Dennis Hastert (R-IL) died at 84 as the highest-ranking U.S. official to ever serve jail time for federal banking crimes.
articles.body: The Purcell County, Illinois, Coroner’s Office says former House Speaker Dennis Hastert, R-Ill., "passed away at his home due to natural causes." The brief statement was posted on the coroner’s website early Monday morning. Hastert was 84 and one of the most ignominious figures to serve in American politics. He was the longest-serving Republican speaker in history, wielding the gavel from 1999 to 2007. But Hastert’s career featured one of the most disgraceful falls from grace, becoming the highest-ranking U.S. official to ever do jail time. MONICA LEWINSKY RECALLS 'VERY DARK MOMENTS' AFTER SCANDAL, SURVIVING JUDGMENT BY 'BILLIONS OF STRANGERS' The scandal involving Hastert emerged years after he left Congress — but dates back to the 1960s and 1970s when he served as high school history teacher and wrestling coach in Illinois. Hastert admitted in 2015 that he sexually abused teenage students and athletes as young as 14 — long before he entered Congress in the mid-1980s. Hastert was an accidental speaker. He served as chief deputy whip in the Republican hierarchy in late 1998 when House Speaker Newt Gingrich, R-Ga., decided to step aside. Gingrich was controversial. Some GOP members had knives out for him and believed Gingrich overplayed his hand pushing for impeachment of President Clinton. This, coupled with Republicans nearly losing control of the House in the 1998 midterms, set the table for Gingrich to step aside. Republicans tapped then-Rep. Bob Livingston, R-La., Chairman of the Appropriations Committee, to become Speaker in 1999. But in late 1998, as the House voted to impeach Clinton, it came to light that Livingston had an inappropriate relationship with a lobbyist. Hours before the House voted to approve two articles of impeachment for Clinton linked to his relationship with Monica Lewinsky, Livingston stepped aside and said he would not stand for speaker in the new year. By nightfall, Republicans picked Hastert, a backbencher, to serve as speaker in 1999. Hastert was criticized in late 2006 for not moving more aggressively to protect teenage House pages after it was discovered that then-Rep. Mark Foley, R-Fla., sent inappropriate text messages to the pages. The scandal led to the end of the House page program, which dates back to the beginning of the republic. Hastert lost the speakership when Democrats seized control of the House in the 2006 midterms. Hastert did not serve in the GOP leadership in early 2007 and resigned from office later that year. FMR DEM REP BARNEY FRANK, SHARP-TONGUED LIBERAL TRAILBLAZER AND DODD-FRANK CO-AUTHOR, DIES Hastert was often quiet and shunned interviews and the press. Known as "Coach" to fellow lawmakers because of his wrestling background, Hastert often proclaimed that he was more of a "listener" than a "speaker." But Hastert’s career took a dark turn in 2015. US OLYMPIC HERO NANCY HOGSHEAD WINS LEGAL BATTLE AFTER VOLLEYBALL COACH'S $250M DEFAMATION SUIT IS DISMISSED Federal banking regulators flagged Hastert’s curious withdrawals of staggering amounts of cash at peculiar intervals. Banking regulators suspected the transactions signaled that someone may be blackmailing the former Speaker. But that’s how it came to light that Hastert was actually paying millions of dollars in hush money to the family of a student he abused in the 1970s. Hastert admitted to sexually abusing students decades before at his trial for illegal bank transactions, saying he "mistreated athletes" and "took advantage of him." The judge in the case called the former speaker "a serial child molester." Hastert served 13 of 15 months of his federal sentence for banking crimes at a facility in Rochester, Minn. When Hastert served as speaker, he would not bring a piece of legislation to the floor unless it had the support of a majority of House Republicans. House GOPers continued to use that standard for bills for many years after Hastert left office. But that terminology fell out of favor after Hastert was convicted and information about his past became public.

articles.title: Former Republican House Speaker Dennis Hastert dead at 84
articles.summary: Former Republican Rep. Dennis Hastert, the longest-serving GOP House Speaker, died at 84 after a career marred by his bank fraud conviction.
articles.body: Former Republican Rep. Dennis Hastert, who was the longest-serving GOP House Speaker, died on Monday at the age of 84. Hastert died peacefully of natural causes at his home, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell. The longtime politician represented Illinois' 14th Congressional district for 20 years and served as Speaker of the House for eight years before retiring in 2007. His career was later tarnished by a bank fraud conviction linked to his efforts to quash the story of a former student who accused him of sexual abuse during his time as a high school wrestling coach. He was sentenced to 15 months in prison in 2016. Hastert also underwent sex offender treatment, two years of supervised release after his time behind bars and paid a $250,000 fine to a crime victims fund. Durkin described the then-74-year-old Illinois Republican as a "serial child molester," and that "accusing Individual A of extorting you was unconscionable." Multiple alleged victims and their family members read victim impact statements prior to Hastert's sentencing. But because of the statute of limitations, Hastert could only be charged with a financial crime related to the payments he was making to one of at least four victims of sexual abuse. articles.title: Karoline Leavitt joins Fox News as contributor after leaving White House press secretary role
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt is joining Fox News Channel as a contributor starting in November, bringing her experience as the youngest White House press secretary in history.
articles.body: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is joining Fox News Channel as an on-air contributor, FOX News Media CEO Suzanne Scott announced on Monday. Leavitt, 29, who will provide commentary across the Fox News lineup, starts on Nov. 1. She most recently served as the 36th White House press secretary during President Donald Trump’s second administration, from January 2025 until August 2026. "Karoline’s firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today’s political landscape. I look forward to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House press secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defined my tenure, to Fox’s millions of viewers across their many platforms." Leavitt served as a spokesperson for MAGA Inc., before joining Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and later becoming the youngest White House press secretary in history. articles.summary: El analista político habla de que el anuncio les pilla a contrapié: "La convocatoria puede pillar por sorpresa para sacar ventaja sobre tus adversarios, no sobre tus socios"
articles.body: El analista político Antón Losada ha salido al paso tras la noticia bomba del anuncio de elecciones generales para el 29-N. El periodista ha analizado en 'El Pulso de Hoy por Hoy', la candidatura de Sumar para las próximas elecciones convocadas el próximo 29 de noviembre. Y, de paso, ha centrado su análisis en la izquierda y lo que sucede. Ha señalado directamente a Sumar y que este anuncio la haya llegado con el pie cambiado. Ha indicado que el nuevo 'Frente Amplio' que tenía como fecha límite el próximo 17 de octubre para saber su candidato y su programa... pero la situación ocurrida este lunes hace que no pueda esperar más para presentar a su candidata. Los resultados de las próximas elecciones dependen "absolutamente de ellos", señala el experto. "Efectivamente, si quieren competir en las elecciones y quiere demostrar que son más lo primero que tienen que hacer es acelerar sus propios pasos porque esto depende absolutamente de ellos". Y añade que la convocatoria de elecciones "normalmente" busca "pillar desprevenido o por sorpresa para sacar ventaja sobre tus adversarios, no sobre tus socios". De hecho, Losada ha puesto en la diana lo que le sucede a la izquierda. Porque ha explicado que la situación de la izquierda viene marcada por "la desunión, líos, peleas, rupturas y reencuentros en los últimos 10 años". Y ha recalcado que "difícilmente el votante de izquierdas va a votar a los mismos que han llevado a ese espacio a la situación actual". Y ha indicado que este momento inestable de lo que ocurre en Sumar y su 'coalición' no es una responsabilidad de Sánchez ni del PSOE porque es "el espacio a su izquierda es el que necesita acelerar los plazos, clarificar el discurso y presentar un cuadro de candidatos".

articles.title: Dennis Hastert, disgraced former House speaker, dies at 84
articles.summary: Former Speaker of the House Dennis Hastert represented Illinois for two decades in Congress and was later jailed on charges related to his concealment of hus...
articles.body:
Washington — Former Speaker of the House Dennis Hastert, who represented Illinois for two decades in Congress and was jailed for violating banking laws, has died, a coroner in Illinois said. He was 84.

Both the longest-serving Republican House speaker and the highest-ranking elected U.S. official to serve a prison sentence, Hastert's stunning fall from grace came in 2016, when he was sentenced to 15 months in prison on charges related to his concealment of hush money payments made to cover up his sexual abuse of teenage boys during his time as a high school wrestling coach.

Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell confirmed Monday that Hastert died at his home over the weekend due to natural causes. No further details were given.

Born in 1942 in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert grew up in a farming community. He went on to graduate from Wheaton College, where he received a degree in economics, before earning a teaching degree from Northern Illinois University. Hastert married Jean Kahl in 1973. The couple had two sons.

Hastert worked as a teacher in Illinois for 16 years while coaching wrestling. In 1976, he was named Illinois Coach of the Year. Four decades later, he would admit to sexually abusing boys during his time as a coach.

Hastert then served in the Illinois legislature, before going on to be elected to represent Illinois' 14th district in the U.S. House in 1986.

Hastert served in Congress from 1987 to 2007. With the mentorship of House Minority Leader Robert. H Michel, Hastert's profile grew among the GOP ranks, and in 1995, he became chief deputy whip. When former House Speaker Newt Gingrich stepped down in 1998, Hastert became the conference's second choice for his successor, following Rep. Bob Livingston's decision to step aside amid a scandal over extra-marital affairs.

Known as the "accidental speaker," Hastert would go on to become the longest-serving Republican speaker in history. During his tenure, Hastert, who had been a vocal critic of the Clinton administration, worked closely with former President George W. Bush on his policy agenda.

Among Hastert's most enduring imprints on the chamber is the rule that bears his name, which informally requires that the House vote only on measures that have a majority of support from the majority party in the chamber. The rule, which has faced criticism for making Congress more partisan, has posed hurdles for Republican House leadership in recent years.

After House Republicans lost the majority in the 2006 midterm elections, Hastert opted to leave leadership, before resigning from Congress in 2007.

Hastert became a lobbyist and consultant after leaving office. In 2013, the FBI and IRS began investigating the former speaker surrounding suspicions that he was illegally structuring bank transactions. In 2015, Hastert was indicted for structuring bank transactions to evade reporting requirements and making false statements to the FBI.

Hastert pleaded guilty in 2015 to violating banking laws by making repeated large cash withdrawals, which were revealed to be going to one of his victims. During the hearing, Hastert admitted to sexually abusing boys during his time as their wrestling coach. At his sentencing, U.S. District Judge Thomas M. Durkin called Hastert a "serial child molester," and sentenced him to 15 months in prison, a $250,000 fine and ordered him to participate in a sex offender program. Hastert was not charged with sex-related crimes, as the statutes of limitations had expired. He served 13 months in a federal prison before his release in 2017.

Zachary Farden, the U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Illinois, said after Hastert was sentenced that there are "no winners in any of this"

"Mr. Hastert's legend and legacy are gone, and in its place are a broken, humiliated man," Farden said. "That is how it should be."
